extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of periodical essays, journalists, schoolmasters and educated public (early 18th‑century English readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for writing clear, responsible periodical prose and for related public conduct (language use in newspapers, moral responsibility of authors, schoolmasterly pedagogy, and decorum in public assemblies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid foreign (French) phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: I have often wished ... certain Men might be set apart as Superintendants of our Language, to hinder any Words of a Foreign Coin from passing among us; and in particular to prohibit any French Phrases from becoming Current in this Kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The present War has so Adulterated our Tongue with strange Words ... Our Soldiers ... want Words in their own Tongue to tell us what it is they Atchieve, and therefore send us over Accounts ... in a Jargon of Phrases, which they learn among their Conquered Enemies. Use English alternatives when native words suffice; avoid importing foreign terms that make narratives unintelligible. Example antipattern: a young officer's letter full of French military phrases that his father and parish curate cannot understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plain English and clarity in reporting (especially war accounts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The English cannot be too clear in their Narrative of those Actions ... our Papers are filled with so many unintelligible Exploits, and the French obliged to lend us a Part of their Tongue before we can know how they are Conquered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer vernacular idiom in histories and news so readers of ordinary sense can follow events; explain military or technical matters in accessible language. Example: the father who could not understand his son's fashionable military 'jargon' until the same terms appeared in newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors must consider the permanence and public effect of their writings
rubrics_metrics.description: If Writings are thus durable ... how careful should an Author be of committing any thing to Print that may corrupt Posterity, and poison the Minds of Men with Vice and Error?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize books as long‑lasting legacies: avoid committing corrupting ideas to print. The essay argues authors should not publish material that will 'corrupt Posterity' and that authors of vice are 'the Pests of Society.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not season vicious sentiments with wit (moral responsibility of writers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers of great Talents, who employ their Parts in propagating Immorality, and seasoning vicious Sentiments with Wit and Humour, are to be looked upon as the Pests of Society, and the Enemies of Mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using humour or cleverness to make immoral ideas attractive; the piece portrays such writers as actively harmful and morally culpable. Anecdote: an atheist author terrified of his own book's influence is comforted by a curate who suggests the book is harmless because it is weak — but the admonition stands: don't publish to seduce the age into vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness andavoidance of forced or invented falsehoods in narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: The same ungoverned Fancy ... makes the Author of the following Letter do the same in Private; one is a Prating, the other a Silent Liar. There is little pursued in the Errors of either of these Worthies, but mere present Amusement ... the Folly of him who lets his Fancy place him in distant Scenes untroubled and uninterrupted, is very much preferable to that of him who is ever forcing a Belief, and defending his Untruths with new Inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from inventing false incidents to enliven plain narrative or forcing readers to believe fabricated details. Fantastical embellishment that misleads (prating or lying) is criticized; prefer honest, restrained presentation over concocted 'castle‑building' stories that deceive or falsely aggrandize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance imagination with reason; avoid letting fancy cause real harm
rubrics_metrics.description: A Castle‑builder ... erect their Structures in the most unstable of Elements, the Air ... the least Breath of Wind has often demolished my magnificent Edifices ... The ill Consequence of these Reveries is inconceivably great, seeing the loss of imaginary Possessions makes Impressions of real Woe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination and day‑dreams should be tempered by economy and rational planning: unchecked fantasies can cause practical mismanagement, emotional distress and bad economy. The correspondent asks for a method to 'settle my Head and cool my Brain‑pan.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachers (schoolmasters) should instruct politely and avoid cruel correction
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a worthy Attempt to undertake the Cause of distrest Youth; ... If you can disarm them of their Rods, you will certainly have your old Age reverenced ... 'Tis pity but we had a Set of Men, polite in their Behaviour and Method of Teaching, who should be put into a Condition of being above flattering or fearing the Parents ... We might then possibly see Learning become a Pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogy should be gentle, civilized and not reliant on corporal punishment; make learning pleasurable so children do not 'abhor' it. Avoid barbarous severity that breaks spirits — examples given of children whipped for trivial mistakes. Recommended: instructors of good manners and method, secure from parental pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain decorum in public assemblies; punish or surcharge disturbers
rubrics_metrics.description: For preserving therefore the Decency of publick Assemblies, methinks it would be but reasonable that those who Disturb others should pay at least a double Price for their Places; or rather Women of Birth and Distinction should be informed that a Levity of Behaviour ... degrades them below their meanest Attendants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate practical measures to keep order (e.g., higher price for those who disturb) and social admonition: members of the genteel classes should avoid frivolous behaviour that disrupts others. Examples: whispering sets, loud laughers, footmen behaving coarsely at plays.
